body_markdown:
Most FUTA and SUTA errors don't happen at the math step. They happen earlier, when a worker gets misclassified, a wage gets miscapped, an exemption gets missed, or a multi-state nexus change goes untracked. By the time you're running the actual $7,000 wage-base calculation, the input is usually already wrong. Four classification patterns account for most of the FUTA and SUTA exposure mixed-workforce employers carry into[Form 940](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-form-940) season, and each one is diagnosable during a pre-filing review, well before an agency notice would ever surface it.


## Worker Classification Comes Before Any Wage Calculation


The single most expensive FUTA mistake starts before payroll ever runs a number: treating a worker as a contractor when the IRS's common-law control test would classify them as an employee. If you later reclassify that worker, FUTA liability follows the correct classification rather than whatever label your payroll system had on file, and the correction typically reaches back to the date the misclassification began, creating retroactive FUTA liability for that entire period.


A narrower but just as costly version of this mistake trips up seasonal and part-time staff specifically. "Part-time" describes a work schedule. It carries no tax classification of its own under FUTA. If you employ someone part-time or seasonally and they meet the definition of an employee, their wages are fully FUTA-taxable up to the $7,000 wage base, exactly like a full-time employee's. There's no seasonal or part-time carve-out in the statute itself; the exemptions that do exist (covered below) turn on entity type or payment category, never on how many hours someone works or how long their engagement lasts.


A third classification wrinkle applies specifically to family employment. Wages paid to your child under age 21 for services performed in your trade or business are exempt from FUTA, and a similar exemption applies to wages paid to your spouse, but both exemptions depend on business structure. They apply when the business is a sole proprietorship, or in the child's case, a partnership in which each partner is a parent of the child. The moment that business incorporates or becomes an LLC taxed as a corporation, the exemption disappears, because the employing entity is now legally separate from its owners even though the owners are still family. A growth-stage founder who incorporates mid-year and keeps paying a teenage child or a spouse under the same informal arrangement can lose this exemption without ever changing the paycheck itself, simply because the entity behind the paycheck changed.


Getting worker classification right at the point of hire, rather than revisiting it at filing time, is the highest-leverage fix available here, and it extends to family employment arrangements as much as to contractor and part-time calls. Because Asure specialists handle payroll tax filing and reporting as part of the engagement, with you remaining the employer of record throughout, worker classification gets confirmed against the IRS's own test before a first paycheck runs instead of surfacing as a gap during an audit. Once worker type is settled correctly, the next classification layer is the wage itself. Not every dollar you pay a confirmed employee is FUTA-taxable.


## Not Every Dollar Paid to an Employee Is a FUTA-Taxable Wage


Certain payments are excluded from FUTA wages entirely, and the exclusions are where mixed-workforce employers most often overpay without realizing it. Employer-paid health insurance premiums and HSA contributions are excluded from FUTA wages, per[IRS Publication 15-B](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p15b) . Dependent care assistance is excluded too, up to a cap that increased meaningfully for 2026. The Dependent Care Assistance Program exclusion rose from $5,000 to **$7,500** per year under the[One Big Beautiful Bill Act](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/house-bill/1) , a change that took effect for 2026, holds as of August 2026, and is not indexed for inflation going forward. An employer still budgeting FUTA exposure against the old $5,000 figure is overstating their own liability on this specific line item.


The exclusion is narrower than it sounds, though. "Company-paid benefits" is not a single, monolithic FUTA-exempt category. Cash fringe benefits and non-qualified perks are taxable; the exclusion covers specific, named categories like health coverage, HSA contributions, and dependent care assistance within its cap, and it stops there. Treating the exclusion as broader than it actually is produces the opposite mistake: an employer who assumes a cash perk is FUTA-exempt because it's labeled a "benefit" underpays FUTA on that line and inherits the liability later.


Retirement contributions split the same way, and the same Publication 15-B guidance that covers the health and dependent-care exclusions above governs this split too. An employee's own elective deferral into a 401(k) plan is still treated as FUTA wages. Deferring salary into a retirement account doesn't remove it from the wage base; it just changes where the money sits. The employer's matching contribution works the opposite way. Employer contributions to a qualified retirement plan aren't wages to the employee at all, so they never enter the FUTA calculation in the first place. Confusing these two directions, treating an employee's own deferral as excluded, or treating the employer match as taxable, produces the same kind of wage-base error as a health-benefit or dependent-care misclassification, just on the retirement side of the ledger.


The **$7,000** wage-base cap itself works differently from either exclusion above, and differently again from the retirement-contribution split just described. It applies per employee, per calendar year, across all wages combined, as a single running total rather than a series of separate limits. A multi-location employer paying the same employee from two different payroll runs still caps that employee's FUTA-taxable wages at $7,000 total for the year; the cap doesn't reset per location or per pay cycle. AsureCentral tracks FUTA-taxable wages against this single annual cap in the same connected system that runs payroll itself, so a wage-base cap doesn't get double-applied or missed because two different teams were tracking two different payroll streams. Wage-level exclusions are one classification layer. Entity-level exemptions are a separate one, and for certain organizations, the exemption applies before any wage calculation begins at all.


## Entity-Level Exemptions Require Their Own Compliance Track


Nonprofits and household employers each carry an entity-level FUTA question, and the two are easy to conflate even though they work completely differently. A 501(c)(3) nonprofit is exempt from FUTA outright. That exemption does not automatically extend to SUTA, though; SUTA treatment for nonprofits is state-dependent, and many states offer a choice between the standard contributory method and a reimbursing method, where the nonprofit pays the state back dollar-for-dollar for unemployment claims actually paid out rather than paying an ongoing tax rate. The reimbursing election can look attractive on paper, but it carries real cash-flow risk: a nonprofit with seasonal or high-turnover staffing can face a large, lump-sum SUTA bill the moment a former employee successfully files an unemployment claim, a cost that contributory employers spread out instead of absorbing all at once.


Household employment runs on an entirely different track from standard Form 940 filing, and it's the FUTA category most likely to go unreported among growth-stage founders who also employ a nanny, a household manager, or other domestic staff. If you pay cash wages to household employees totaling **$1,000** or more in any calendar quarter of 2025 or 2026, the first $7,000 of wages paid to each household employee in 2026 becomes FUTA-taxable, but this liability is reported on[Schedule H of your personal Form 1040](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-schedule-h-form-1040) rather than on Form 940. A business owner who correctly files Form 940 for their company's W-2 staff can still miss this obligation entirely if they don't realize household payroll runs through a completely separate filing mechanism.


Entity-level exemptions are fixed by organizational structure and don't change from one payroll run to the next. Multi-state SUTA exposure is the opposite: it's dynamic, and it shifts every time a remote employee changes their work location.


## Multi-State SUTA Is a Nexus and Wage-Base Tracking Problem


Remote workforce growth has turned SUTA from a single-state calculation into a multi-jurisdiction wage-base management problem for a lot of employers who didn't have one a few years ago. State SUTA wage bases vary enormously, and the range keeps widening. Washington's 2026 wage base is **$78,200** as of August 2026, the current national high, up from $72,800 in 2025, while several states remain near the $7,000 federal floor. Every state's wage base resets January 1 per employee, independently of every other state's, which means a multi-state employer is tracking as many separate reset dates and caps as there are states with active employees.


A short example shows why this matters in practice. Say an employee earns $50,000 in State A through June, then relocates and earns another $40,000 in State B for the rest of the year. FUTA treats this as one employee with a single $7,000 national cap, already reached early in the year regardless of the move. SUTA generally doesn't work that way. State A owes SUTA tax on that employee's wages up to State A's own wage base for the months worked there, and in most states, State B separately owes SUTA tax on wages up to State B's own wage base once the employee starts working there, without automatic credit for wages already taxed in State A. An employer who assumes the federal $7,000 logic carries over to SUTA can end up under-remitting to the second state, over-remitting relative to the first, or both, depending on which state's wage base is higher.


The FUTA credit-reduction mechanism adds a second layer that most payroll systems don't auto-flag. Employers in a state with an outstanding federal unemployment loan balance owe additional FUTA on[Form 940 Schedule A](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-schedule-a-form-940) , on top of the standard rate, until that state's loan is repaid. The IRS publishes the list of credit-reduction states each November, and that list changes from cycle to cycle. As of August 2026, employers should confirm the current-year list directly rather than assume it matches a prior year's, since an employer operating in a listed state owes the adjustment regardless of whether that specific employer's own SUTA payments were made on time.


A remote employee who relocates mid-year creates a SUTA nexus change that has to be reflected in state registrations and wage-base tracking in the new state; a payroll system's address field alone doesn't capture it. AsureCentral surfaces this kind of liability-trigger change as an exception for review rather than a silent data update, with Luna AI, embedded across the platform, flagging the shift using real payroll data so it gets a human's attention instead of quietly changing a state code with no one noticing. ## Bottom Line


FUTA and SUTA compliance failures are classification problems, not calculation problems, and they cluster into four predictable patterns:


- **Worker classification** : treating an employee as a contractor, assuming a part-time or seasonal carve-out that doesn't exist, or missing a family-employment exemption.
- **Wage-base and exclusion errors** : misapplying the $7,000 FUTA cap, or miscounting which benefits, retirement contributions, or dependent-care payments are actually excluded.
- **Entity-level exemptions** : overlooking nonprofit FUTA/SUTA treatment or missing the separate Schedule H filing track for household employees.
- **Multi-state SUTA nexus** : losing track of wage-base resets, registration requirements, and credit-reduction status as employees relocate.


Each pattern is diagnosable before you file, well ahead of the agency notice that would otherwise surface it. Building a classification-first review into your pre-filing workflow, confirming worker type, checking which wages are actually excluded, verifying entity-level exemptions apply the way you assume, and tracking SUTA nexus changes as they happen, catches the errors that trigger audits. Treating Form 940 as a math exercise catches them after the fact, usually as an agency notice. ## Related Questions


### What payments are exempt from FUTA tax?


The major exclusion categories are certain fringe benefits (employer-paid health insurance, HSA contributions, dependent care assistance up to $7,500 for 2026 under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act), wages paid by an exempt nonprofit, and payments to independent contractors who are correctly classified as such.[Form 940 Schedule A](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-schedule-a-form-940) is where any related credit-reduction adjustment gets reported.


### Do contractors count toward FUTA liability?


No, but only if the classification is correct. The IRS's common-law control test determines whether a worker is actually a contractor or an employee; the label on a contract carries no weight on its own. A misclassified contractor creates retroactive FUTA liability back to the date the misclassification began.


### How does the $7,000 FUTA wage base work across the year?


It's a per-employee, per-calendar-year cap that applies across all wages combined, as a single running total rather than a series of separate limits by pay period or by state. A multi-state employer tracks this cap once across every state's payroll for that same employee, combining wages from every state into the same $7,000 total.


### Are nonprofits exempt from FUTA and SUTA?


501(c)(3) nonprofits are exempt from FUTA. SUTA exemption varies by state, and many states let a nonprofit choose between the standard contributory rate and a reimbursing election. The reimbursing election carries real cash-flow risk, since it can produce a large lump-sum bill when a former employee's unemployment claim is approved, rather than spreading that cost out over time the way the contributory method does.


### How does SUTA work for remote employees in multiple states?


SUTA generally follows the employee's actual work location, which for a remote employee is typically their home state. A location change mid-year requires registering in the new state and tracking that state's own wage base and reset date going forward, plus checking whether that state carries a FUTA credit-reduction status that adds to your federal liability on[Form 940 Schedule A](https://www.irs.gov/forms-pubs/about-schedule-a-form-940) .
